raw_text:
The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity in which contrast opacification of the distal coronary tree is delayed despite absent or non-obstructive epicardial coronary disease. It was first described in 1972 in patients with angina and angiographically normal large coronary arteries [1]. Contemporary diagnosis is usually based on objective thrombolysis in myocardial infarction (TIMI) frame counting, with correction of the longer left anterior descending artery by division by 1.7; a corrected TIMI frame count above 27 frames is commonly used [2]. CSFP should be distinguished from secondary slow flow due to acute coronary syndromes, no-reflow after percutaneous coronary intervention, coronary ectasia, spasm, air embolism, severe ventricular dysfunction, valvular disease, or connective-tissue disorders.

Pathobiology remains heterogeneous. Early biopsy studies in angina with patent epicardial arteries showed small-vessel fibromuscular hyperplasia, medial hypertrophy, endothelial swelling, and luminal narrowing [3], and later CSFP-specific biopsy work found small-vessel wall thickening, reduced luminal area, mitochondrial abnormalities, and patchy myocardial metabolic changes [4]. Beltrame and colleagues reframed CSFP as a coronary microvascular disorder characterized by recurrent perturbations of microvascular function, with smoking and rest angina prominent clinical associations [5]. Peripheral and coronary endothelial dysfunction also appear central: impaired brachial flow-mediated dilation, reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, increased asymmetric dimethylarginine, and elevated homocysteine have been reported in CSFP cohorts [6–8]. Functional physiology, however, is not uniform. Some studies found impaired coronary flow reserve [9], whereas invasive thermodilution work demonstrated increased resting microvascular resistance with preserved hyperemic reserve [10]. Thus, “slow angiographic transit” may reflect different mixtures of resting arteriolar tone, endothelial dysfunction, diffuse subangiographic atherosclerosis, inflammation, platelet activation, and rheologic factors rather than a single disease mechanism.

Epidemiologically, CSFP is uncommon but not rare among patients referred for angiography for chest pain or suspected ischemia. In a large angiographic series, Hawkins et al. reported a prevalence of 5.5% among patients with normal left ventricular function and normal coronary arteries, with male sex and metabolic syndrome features enriched [11]. Reviews consistently describe a phenotype of relatively younger men, smokers, recurrent chest pain, and frequent acute-care use [12,13]. Yet the condition is also seen in women and in patients meeting broader ischemia-with-no-obstructive-coronary-arteries frameworks. Recent work cautions against equating visual slow flow with invasively proven coronary microvascular dysfunction in all patients [14]. Intracoronary imaging and physiologic studies further suggest that diffuse, angiographically “hidden” atherosclerosis may contribute in selected cases [15].

Clinically, CSFP most often presents with recurrent angina, frequently at rest, and may mimic unstable angina or myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries. Cross-sectional and follow-up cohorts document repeated hospitalizations and persistent symptoms [16,17]. Noninvasive stress tests and perfusion imaging may be abnormal, supporting true ischemia in some patients [18]. Although prognosis is generally better than obstructive coronary disease, CSFP should not be dismissed as benign: case reports and electrocardiographic studies link CSFP with QT/P-wave dispersion, atrial arrhythmia susceptibility, ventricular arrhythmias, and rare sudden cardiac death [19,20]. Platelet indices, inflammatory markers, and homocysteine have been investigated as accessible correlates of angiographic severity, but their diagnostic specificity remains limited [21–24].

Management is empirical because large randomized outcome trials are lacking. Risk-factor modification is rational, particularly smoking cessation, blood pressure and lipid control, weight management, and treatment of insulin resistance or metabolic syndrome. Nitrates are often disappointing and may theoretically worsen flow by preferential epicardial dilation without improving microvascular resistance. Small studies suggest symptomatic or physiologic benefit from calcium-channel blockade, including sustained-release diltiazem [25], and from beta-blockade with nebivolol, possibly via nitric-oxide-mediated endothelial effects and improved exercise parameters [26,27]. Dipyridamole can improve perfusion or angiographic runoff in selected patients [18,28]. Hyperbaric oxygen and other endothelial-targeted strategies remain investigational [29]. Emerging transcriptomic and microRNA data indicate inflammatory and endothelial regulatory pathways that may eventually refine phenotyping and therapy [30]. For now, CSFP is best considered a measurable angiographic sign with diverse mechanisms; careful exclusion of secondary causes, objective frame-count documentation, attention to microvascular angina, and individualized antianginal and preventive therapy are the practical pillars of care.
